title: Loverboy
full_review:
Emily Stoll is the ultimate possessive mother in the bleak if well-acted adaptation of Victoria Redel's novel, "Loverboy" (THINKFilm).

The psychotic Emily (Kyra Sedgwick) was emotionally scarred in childhood, as we learn from flashbacks where her amoral, self-absorbed parents (played by the film's director, Kevin Bacon, and Marisa Tomei) virtually ignored her.

The adult Emily has no use for a husband, but is determined to get herself pregnant, and have a child who can live with her in a totally insulated world. After a series of quickie encounters, a liaison with a flirtatious businessman (Campbell Scott) results in the birth of Paul, played beautifully by 8-year-old Dominic Scott Kay.

Her relationship with the child -- whom she calls "loverboy" to the boy's disdain -- is all-consuming, and she does her best to keep him out of school (against the boy's own wishes), and apart from any other social interaction, all the while desperately keeping him engaged in stimulating activities.

But a sinister air permeates all, as the action is framed by Emily keeping the boy behind the wheel of a locked car, ostensibly giving him driving lessons, but before long telling him they must sleep in the car overnight. Knowing this setup, it's difficult to accept Emily -- with her clearly dangerous eccentricity -- as the vibrant, Auntie Mame-like nonconformist for which we're supposed to give her at least partial credit.

Bacon's big-screen directorial debut shows skill, and he's assembled a first-rate cast including Blair Brown as a friendly neighbor, Matt Dillon as a geologist who shows an interest in the boy (and later Emily), Sandra Bullock as the woman Emily idolized as a child but who suddenly left town without a word, and Oliver Platt and Melissa Errico as concerned school employees.

But the film's good elements are outweighed by a basically unlikable protagonist (Sedgwick's nuanced performance notwithstanding) and a fairly predictable -- relentlessly downbeat -- plot.

Some of the sexual elements of the film -- particularly as Emily endeavors to get herself pregnant -- are sordid, if perhaps dramatically valid. Emily's frequent kissing of Paul on the lips has an intentionally unsavory patina, but it seems more a case "smother love" stemming from past abandonment issues, rather than signaling actual incest.

Fans of Sedgwick's TV drama, "The Closer," may find her unhinged portrayal here intriguing, but the setup never quite rings true, and even at 86 minutes "Loverboy" outstays its welcome.

The film contains promiscuity, some brief sexual encounters, artificial insemination, partial rear and upper female nudity, breastfeeding, some crude language, an act of animal cruelty, suicide, and a murder attempt. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
